newsitem.title: UK: More troops en route to troubled N.Ireland.
newsitem.headline: More troops en route to troubled N.Ireland.

text.p: Hundreds more British troops were on their way to Northern Ireland on Thursday to help police as trouble loomed over two more disputed Protestant parades.
Catholic leaders from the two cities urged their supporters to turn up in their thousands to prevent what they see as sectarian, triumphalist parades on their doorsteps on Saturday.

The Orange Order was reported by political sources to be under intense pressure to modify their proposed marches down Belfast's Lower Ormeau Road and the city centre of Londonderry but there was no sign it would agree to any change.

The centuries-old Order says it is being wrongly blamed for the violence which flared after Sunday's march along the Catholic Garvaghy Road and wants only to hold peaceful marches to celebrate its Protestant faith and British loyalty.

A wave of car hijackings, petrol bomb attacks and armed attacks on security forces appeared to have ebbed early on Thursday after some of the worst violence in Northern Ireland since civil rights marches in the 1970s.
"It's much quieter. But I get the feeling it's only half time," said one security source.

Police were investigating two suspicious dustbins left under a bridge near Dungannon on Wednesday after a caller claimed they had been left by Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas fighting British rule of the province.
There was no way of knowing yet if the bins contained explosive or were merely hoaxes designed to stretch security forces ahead of the weekend parades, security sources said.

Britain said it was sending between 400 and 500 more troops to the province to "combat terrorism and help maintain law and order" and back up the beleaguered Royal Ulster Constabulary police who are in the front line against the unrest.

Gerry Adams, president of Sinn Fein, the political wing of the IRA, maintained a barrage of criticism at Britain's handling of the march issue but appealed to his Catholic supporters not to sully the community's image with riots and petrol-bombing.
"We have to maintain the focus on where it should be and that is the British government's treatment of Nationalists who are being deprived of their rights," he said.

He was speaking to reporters at a rally in the Garvaghy Road area of Portadown, scene of the Sunday Orange Order parade which sparked the initial violence after police and troops saturated the area to hurry the parade through, unhindered by protest.
Up to 5,000 Catholics attended the rally, which was watched by about 400 troops and police at a discreet distance.

Gerard Rice, the Ormeau Road residents association spokesman, appealed to "right-thinking Catholics across Ireland to stop work for two hours on Friday" in an island-wide protest at Britain's handling of contentious parades.
He joined his opposite number in Londonderry, a stronghold of militant Irish nationalism, in urging people to turn up in their thousands on Saturday to prevent the twin parades.
They are being staged on July 12, which marks the anniversary of a Protestant battle victory over a Catholic King which Protestants see as a landmark in entrenching their presence in Ireland.
Saturday's parade is the first by the Orange Order in Londonderry for five years. Upwards of 10,000 Orangemen are expected to take part.
"We have been marching in this city for many years. We have given no offence," an Orange official said.
In London, Prime Minister Tony Blair pledged not to give up the search for peace in Northern Ireland and came out in support of his beleaguered Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam.

"I am not going to give up on Northern Ireland. I am going to carry on searching for a solution and I believe if there were true good will on all sides and a little bit of give and take and understanding a solution could be found," Blair said.
